name: Data Science & AI
notes: Competency areas from the PA FBLA 2026-2027 Data Science & AI guidelines (updated August 2026), knowledge areas and study-guide item counts: https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/26-27-Data-Science-AI-PA.pdf . The brief asked for 2025-26; the fbla.org 2025-26 page returned 403 and no 2025-26 knowledge-area list was retrievable, so these are the current-cycle areas. Format per the same guideline: 100 multiple-choice questions, 50 minutes, no points deducted. Question counts per area follow the guideline (15/15/10/10/10/10/10/20). Re-check against the 2025-26 guideline if its wording differs. Calculations were recomputed by hand; all items are original.
subs: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: What is the range of the dataset 4, 8, 8, 15, 21?
questions.explain: Range is the maximum minus the minimum, 21 - 4 = 17. The mean of 11.2 is a different measure, a trap for students who mix up terms.

questions.q: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by a single extreme outlier?
questions.explain: The mean uses every value, so one extreme value pulls it. The median and mode are resistant to outliers.

questions.q: The values 2, 4, and 6 are treated as a sample. What is the sample variance (divide the sum of squared deviations by n - 1)?
questions.explain: The mean is 4, the squared deviations are 4, 0, 4 (sum 8), and 8 / (3 - 1) = 4. Dividing by n gives 2.67, the population variance.

questions.q: A dataset has a standard deviation of 0. What does this mean?
choices: All values in the dataset are identical
questions.explain: Standard deviation measures spread. A value of zero means there is no spread at all, so every value is the same.

questions.q: In a normal (Gaussian) distribution, about what percentage of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explain: The 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% within one SD, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three. The 95% figure is the two-SD trap.

questions.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is the expected value of the number shown?
questions.explain: The expected value is the average of the outcomes weighted by probability: (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. It is not itself a possible roll.

questions.q: A raffle ticket costs $2. It pays $50 with probability 0.02 and pays nothing otherwise. What is the expected net gain per ticket?
questions.explain: Expected payout is 0.02 x $50 = $1.00. Subtracting the $2 cost gives an expected net of -$1.00 per ticket.

questions.q: The number of customers who enter a store on a Monday (0, 1, 2, 3, ...) is which type of variable?
questions.explain: Counts that take separate whole-number values are discrete. Continuous variables can take any value within an interval.

questions.q: A survey asks people to rate service as poor, fair, good, or excellent. What type of variable is this?
questions.explain: The categories have a meaningful order but the gaps between them are not necessarily equal, which defines an ordinal variable.

questions.q: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A and B)?
questions.explain: Independent events multiply: 0.3 x 0.5 = 0.15. Adding the probabilities (0.80) is the trap for students who confuse AND with OR.

questions.q: The covariance between two variables is positive. What does this indicate?
choices: The variables tend to move in the same direction
questions.explain: A positive covariance means the variables tend to rise and fall together. It does not prove causation, and its size depends on units, unlike correlation.

questions.q: What is the median of the dataset 9, 3, 7, 1, 5, 11?
questions.explain: Sorted: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values, (5 + 7) / 2 = 6.

questions.q: Which statement about the normal distribution is correct?
choices: It is always skewed to the right
Its mean is always larger than its median
It is symmetric and bell-shaped, with mean, median, and mode equal
It applies only to discrete data
questions.explain: A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so the mean, median, and mode coincide. Skewed distributions are the ones with unequal measures.

questions.q: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
questions.explain: First draw: 3/5. Second draw with one fewer marble: 2/4. Product is 6/20 = 3/10. The 9/25 answer is what you get with replacement, which is the trap.

questions.q: Which problem is the most direct cause of sampling bias?
choices: A sample size that is too large
Reporting results to two decimal places
A sample that does not represent the population, such as surveying only online volunteers
Using a spreadsheet instead of a calculator
questions.explain: Sampling bias occurs when some members of the population are systematically more or less likely to be selected, so the sample is unrepresentative.

questions.q: Which visual is best for showing the distribution of a single continuous variable?
questions.explain: A histogram bins a continuous variable and shows how often values fall in each range. A scatterplot is for two variables.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: What five values does a boxplot display?
questions.explain: A boxplot shows the five-number summary: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which diagram is best for examining the relationship between two numeric variables?
questions.explain: A scatterplot places each observation as a point on two numeric axes, which reveals association, trend, and outliers.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: When is multiple linear regression used?
choices: To predict a yes or no category from one variable
To predict a numeric outcome from two or more predictor variables
To group unlabeled data into clusters
To find the most frequent value in a dataset
questions.explain: Multiple linear regression models a numeric outcome using several predictors. Predicting a binary category is logistic regression.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which technique predicts a binary outcome, such as approved or denied?
questions.explain: Logistic regression models the probability of a binary class. Linear regression predicts continuous values and k-means does not use labels.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a data quality problem?
choices: A table with a clear data dictionary
Dates stored in one consistent format
A relational database with defined keys
questions.explain: Duplicate records, along with missing values and low-quality sources, are common quality problems that reduce analysis reliability.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: 12% of the rows in an income column are missing. Which action is generally the most appropriate first step?
choices: Replace every missing value with zero without checking
Investigate why the values are missing before deciding how to handle them
Drop the column from all future analysis
questions.explain: The cause of missingness (random or systematic) determines whether deletion, imputation, or flagging is valid. Acting before diagnosing can bias results.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which data-cleaning step removes exact repeated rows?
questions.explain: Deduplication identifies and removes duplicate records. The other options transform values rather than remove repeated rows.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which algorithm groups unlabeled data into k clusters by minimizing distance to cluster centroids?
questions.explain: K-means is an unsupervised clustering method that assigns points to the nearest of k centroids and iteratively updates them.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: How does a decision tree decide where to split the data at each node?
choices: By choosing the feature test that best separates the outcome classes
By selecting random splits without testing them
questions.explain: Trees choose splits that maximize class separation, using measures such as Gini impurity or information gain.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which source is least reliable for training a model on public health data?
choices: An anonymous forum post with no citation
A peer-reviewed study with a documented method
A government health survey with a published codebook
questions.explain: Data quality depends on provenance. Uncited, anonymous sources cannot be verified, so they are the least reliable.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: A linear model is y = 2x + 5. What is the predicted y when x = 10?
questions.explain: Substitute: y = 2(10) + 5 = 25. The 52 answer comes from concatenating the digits, a careless error.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: A histogram of house prices is strongly right-skewed. Which measure is the better summary of a typical price?
questions.explain: Extreme high prices pull the mean upward. The median is resistant to those outliers and better represents a typical value in skewed data.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: A scatterplot shows points forming a tight upward diagonal. What does this suggest?
choices: A nonlinear pattern with no trend
questions.explain: Points rising together along a tight line indicate a strong positive linear association. Correlation does not by itself prove causation.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: A model scores 99% on its training data but 70% on new data. What is this pattern most likely showing?
choices: Data leakage in the test set
questions.explain: A large gap between training and new-data performance means the model memorized training patterns that do not generalize, which is overfitting.
questions.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

questions.q: Which SQL clause filters groups after a GROUP BY aggregation?
questions.explain: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters on aggregated results, such as groups whose COUNT exceeds a threshold.

questions.q: Which SQL statement returns only distinct values from a column?
questions.explain: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the result. Other keywords are not standard SQL for this purpose.

questions.q: Which SQL query returns the average salary for each department?
choices: SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept;
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY dept;
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept;
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM employees ORDER BY salary;
questions.explain: AVG with GROUP BY produces one average per department. SUM gives totals, and ORDER BY does not aggregate.

questions.q: Which Python library is primarily used for working with tabular data frames?
questions.explain: Pandas provides the DataFrame structure for loading, cleaning, and analyzing tabular data. PyTorch is for deep learning and Matplotlib is for plotting.

questions.q: Which library is most commonly used to build and train deep neural networks in Python?
questions.explain: PyTorch is a major deep learning framework. Pandas handles data tables, and Matplotlib and Seaborn handle visualization.

questions.q: Which pandas method removes rows containing missing values from a DataFrame df?
questions.explain: dropna() removes rows with missing values by default. fillna() replaces them, drop_duplicates() removes repeats, and isnull() only flags them.

questions.q: Which family of R packages is widely used for data manipulation and visualization?
questions.explain: The tidyverse (including dplyr and ggplot2) is a core R toolkit. Pandas is a Python library, a common trap.

questions.q: Which property ensures a foreign key value refers to an existing primary key row?
questions.explain: Referential integrity requires that every foreign key match an existing primary key or be null. Atomicity is a transaction property.

questions.q: In a relational database, what is a primary key?
choices: A column that must always contain duplicates
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row
Any column that holds numeric data
A table that links two other tables
questions.explain: A primary key uniquely identifies each record and cannot be null. A table that links others is a junction table, a different concept.

questions.q: A table has customer_id, customer_name, and order_id, and customer names repeat across many orders. Which change best applies normalization?
choices: Add customer_name to every order row
Move customers into their own table linked to orders by customer_id
Combine all names into one long text column
questions.explain: Normalization separates repeated entities into their own tables and links them with keys, which removes redundant storage and update anomalies.

questions.q: Generative AI is best described as AI that:
choices: Creates new content such as text, images, or code based on patterns in training data
Only classifies existing data into predefined labels
Stores and retrieves data from a database
Controls physical robots using fixed rules only
questions.explain: Generative models produce new outputs that resemble their training data. Classification alone is a different AI task.

questions.q: Which is a documented limitation of generative AI?
choices: It always cites its sources accurately
It can produce confident but false statements
It never reflects bias from its training data
questions.explain: Generative models can hallucinate, presenting false content fluently. They can also reflect bias present in training data.

questions.q: Which is an example of a use of generative AI in healthcare?
choices: Measuring blood pressure with a manual cuff
Drafting summaries of clinical notes for a physician to review
Scheduling cleaning crews for hospital wings
questions.explain: Generative AI can draft text such as note summaries, which clinicians then review. The other options are not generative AI tasks.

questions.q: Which AI subfield enables a computer to interpret images and video?
questions.explain: Computer vision extracts meaning from visual data such as images and video. NLP handles language.

questions.q: Which AI subfield focuses on enabling computers to understand and generate human language?
questions.explain: Natural language processing covers tasks such as translation, sentiment analysis, and text generation.

questions.q: What does the term large language model (LLM) refer to?
choices: A neural network trained on very large text datasets to predict and generate language
A database that stores every word in a dictionary
A rule-based chatbot with fixed scripts
A spreadsheet tool for analyzing text
questions.explain: LLMs are neural networks trained on large corpora to predict the next token, which lets them generate language. They are not rule-based.

questions.q: Which is a capability of large language models?
choices: Guaranteeing the factual accuracy of every answer
Accessing live data without any tools or retrieval
Physically moving objects in a warehouse
Summarizing long documents and answering questions about them
questions.explain: LLMs are good at summarizing and answering questions from text. They do not guarantee accuracy and cannot access live data without tools.

questions.q: An LLM is asked for a legal case citation and invents one that does not exist. What is this called?
questions.explain: A hallucination is fluent, plausible output that is not grounded in fact. Overfitting and underfitting describe training behavior, not individual outputs.

questions.q: A worker pastes confidential client data into a public LLM service. What is the main risk?
choices: The model will refuse to answer any later question
The data becomes a verified public record
The data may be retained or used for training, creating a privacy exposure
The service will automatically encrypt the data permanently
questions.explain: Data submitted to some services may be stored or used for improvement, so confidential information should not be shared without approval.

questions.q: Which term describes AI that performs a single, narrowly defined task, such as spam filtering?
questions.explain: Narrow (weak) AI is designed for one task. General AI would perform across many tasks at human level, which does not yet exist.

questions.q: What is the core idea of machine learning?
choices: Algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions without a programmer writing every rule
Programmers write every decision rule by hand
Computers store data without processing it
Data is deleted after each analysis to protect privacy
questions.explain: Machine learning infers rules from data rather than relying on hand-coded logic.

questions.q: Which dataset is used to tune hyperparameters and compare candidate models during development?
questions.explain: The validation set guides model selection. The test set is reserved for a final, one-time performance estimate.

questions.q: Which dataset is held out and used only once, at the end, to estimate performance on unseen data?
questions.explain: Using the test set repeatedly for tuning leaks information into the model. It is kept separate for the final estimate.

questions.q: Which learning type uses labeled examples to predict a known outcome?
questions.explain: Supervised learning trains on input-label pairs. Unsupervised learning works without labels.

questions.q: Which learning type improves through rewards and penalties from actions taken in an environment?
questions.explain: Reinforcement learning learns a policy that maximizes cumulative reward through trial and error.

questions.q: A retailer groups customers by purchase behavior with no predefined labels. Which approach fits?
questions.explain: With no labels and a goal of finding natural groups, clustering is an unsupervised method.

questions.q: What is the basic building block of a neural network that combines weighted inputs and applies an activation function?
questions.explain: Each neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs, passes it through an activation function, and sends the output to the next layer.

questions.q: Which description best fits deep learning?
choices: Machine learning that never uses data
Storing large datasets in deep cloud storage
A subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn hierarchical features
Any algorithm that runs on a server
questions.explain: Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks to learn increasingly abstract representations from data.

questions.q: Which description best fits a decision tree?
choices: A method that sorts data into a binary search tree of records
A visual map of all database relationships
A neural network with exactly one layer
A model that splits data by feature tests and ends in leaf nodes that give predictions
questions.explain: Decision trees repeatedly split data on feature tests. Each leaf holds a prediction, which makes the model easy to interpret.

questions.q: A model is 98% accurate on a dataset where 98% of cases are negative because it predicts negative every time. Which measure best reveals its weakness?
questions.explain: Recall measures how many true positives are found. Predicting all negatives gives zero recall on the positive class, exposing the failure that accuracy hides.

questions.q: In predicate logic, the symbol for 'for all' (as in 'for all x, ...') is called what?
questions.explain: The universal quantifier (for all) asserts a property holds for every element. The existential quantifier means 'there exists'.

questions.q: Which predicate logic statement means 'some student passed the exam'?
choices: For all x, if Student(x) then Passed(x)
There exists x such that Student(x) implies Passed(x)
For all x, Student(x) and Passed(x)
There exists x such that Student(x) and Passed(x)
questions.explain: 'Some' uses an existential quantifier combined with AND. Using implication with 'exists' is a trap, since it is true for any non-student.

questions.q: Which of these is a predicate rather than a constant?
questions.explain: A predicate is a property or relation that takes arguments and is true or false. Alex, 42, and seven are constants denoting objects.

questions.q: What is the main difference between logic-based and probability-based reasoning?
choices: Logic-based reasoning uses random sampling; probability-based reasoning uses fixed rules
Logic-based reasoning works only on numbers; probability-based reasoning works only on text
They are identical except for the programming language used
Logic-based reasoning draws certain conclusions from rules; probability-based reasoning assigns degrees of belief to uncertain conclusions
questions.explain: Logic-based systems derive conclusions that follow strictly from rules. Probabilistic systems quantify uncertainty.

questions.q: In a Bayesian network, what do the nodes represent?
questions.explain: Nodes are random variables, and directed edges encode probabilistic dependencies between them.

questions.q: What structural property must the graph underlying a Bayesian network have?
choices: It must be a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
It must be a complete undirected graph
It must be fully connected with every edge bidirectional
It must contain at least one cycle to allow reasoning
questions.explain: A Bayesian network is a DAG, so no variable can depend on itself through a chain of edges. That acyclicity makes the joint probability factor cleanly.

questions.q: A Bayesian network has rain -> wet grass. P(rain) = 0.2, P(wet | rain) = 0.9, and P(wet | no rain) = 0.1. What is P(wet)?
questions.explain: P(wet) = 0.2 x 0.9 + 0.8 x 0.1 = 0.18 + 0.08 = 0.26. Using only the rain case (0.18) ignores the no-rain path.

questions.q: Which is an example of knowledge representation for an AI system?
choices: A list of pixel colors in an image
A semantic network linking 'dog' to 'mammal' with an 'is-a' relation
A random number generator seeded with 42
A table of unsorted sensor readings
questions.explain: Knowledge representation encodes facts and relationships in a form a system can reason over, such as semantic networks or ontologies.

questions.q: Which statement about logic-based AI systems is most accurate?
choices: They require no rules to be written
They cannot represent relationships between objects
They can be explained step by step but struggle with uncertain or incomplete information
questions.explain: Logic systems are transparent and deductive, but they handle uncertainty poorly compared with probabilistic methods.

questions.q: Which predicate logic formula best captures 'Every employee who works overtime is paid extra'?
choices: For all x, (Employee(x) and WorksOvertime(x)) implies PaidExtra(x)
There exists x such that Employee(x) implies (WorksOvertime(x) and PaidExtra(x))
For all x, (Employee(x) or WorksOvertime(x)) implies PaidExtra(x)
For all x, (Employee(x) and PaidExtra(x)) implies WorksOvertime(x)
questions.explain: 'Every' uses a universal quantifier with implication, and the antecedent requires both conditions. The last option reverses the implication, which is the converse error.

questions.q: Which best describes algorithmic bias?
choices: Systematic unfair outcomes that arise when training data or design choices favor some groups over others
Random errors that average out over large datasets
A software bug that only occurs on mobile devices
Deliberate fraud by a software vendor
questions.explain: Algorithmic bias is systematic and tends to disadvantage specific groups. Random error is noise, a different problem.

questions.q: A hiring model trained on past hiring decisions learns to reject applicants from one group. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Historical bias in the training data
Too few hidden layers in the network
A learning rate that is set too high
A test set that is too large
questions.explain: Models trained on biased historical decisions learn and reproduce those patterns. Architecture and hyperparameters do not create the bias.

questions.q: Which privacy risk is specific to large language models?
choices: Slow response times on mobile networks
Storing too many images in a cache
Using too many decimal places in output
Training data memorization that could expose personal information in responses
questions.explain: LLMs can memorize and regurgitate fragments of training data, which may include personal information, so this is a distinct privacy risk.

questions.q: What is a hallucination in the credibility sense?
choices: A deliberate attempt by the model to deceive the user
Fluent output presented as fact that is not supported by the data or sources
A display glitch in the chat interface
questions.explain: Hallucinations are unsupported outputs that read as confident fact. The model is not intentionally deceiving anyone.

questions.q: Which is an ethical dilemma raised by self-driving vehicles?
choices: Which fuel type should be used for charging
How the vehicle should act in unavoidable collision scenarios
What color the vehicle body should be
Which songs the radio should play
questions.explain: Self-driving systems raise hard questions about harm and responsibility in unavoidable crashes, a recognized ethical dilemma.

questions.q: Which practice best protects privacy when using personal data to train a model?
choices: Collect all available data so the model is more accurate
Keep all data indefinitely in case it is useful later
Publish raw data publicly to allow peer review
Data minimization: collect and keep only the data needed for the purpose
questions.explain: Data minimization limits exposure by collecting and retaining only what is necessary, a core fair information practice.

questions.q: What is a proxy variable in the context of algorithmic bias?
choices: A seemingly neutral feature, such as zip code, that correlates with a protected characteristic
A duplicate copy of the training set
The variable the model is trained to predict
The output of an unsupervised algorithm
questions.explain: Proxies let a model reproduce discrimination without using a protected attribute directly, because the neutral feature carries the same information.

questions.q: Which principle, in widely used fair information practices, requires that personal data be used only for the purpose it was collected for?
questions.explain: Use limitation restricts secondary use of personal data without consent. Portability and erasure are individual rights, and anonymization is a technique.

questions.q: A company removes names from a dataset but keeps zip code, birth date, and sex. Why might individuals still be identifiable?
choices: Removing names makes the data fully anonymous under U.S. law
Zip codes are always encrypted in modern datasets
Those combined quasi-identifiers can be linked to public records to re-identify people
Birth dates are never considered personal information
questions.explain: Combinations of quasi-identifiers can uniquely identify many people when linked to other data. Removing direct identifiers alone does not guarantee anonymity.

questions.q: Which is a common ethical concern about AI-generated images?
choices: They always require a larger file size than photographs
They may imitate artists' styles or use training images without consent
They cannot be displayed in public spaces
They are always identical to their training data
questions.explain: Concerns include consent, attribution, and imitation of creators' work. Generated images are not automatically copies of training data.

questions.q: Which is an example of structured data?
choices: Rows and columns in a sales table with fixed fields
Audio recordings from a call center
questions.explain: Structured data fits a predefined schema of rows and columns with fixed fields. The others lack that fixed tabular structure.

questions.q: Which is an example of unstructured data?
choices: A table of order IDs and prices
A collection of customer emails with free-form text
A database of employee names and hire dates
questions.explain: Free-form text does not follow a fixed schema, so it is unstructured. The other options are tabular, hence structured.

questions.q: Which value is categorical rather than numeric?
questions.explain: Eye color is a label with no numeric meaning. The others are measured or counted numbers.

questions.q: What is the decimal number 255 in hexadecimal?
questions.explain: 255 = 15 x 16 + 15, so each digit is F, giving FF. F0 is 240, a common arithmetic slip.

questions.q: What is the binary representation of decimal 10?
questions.explain: 10 = 8 + 2, which is 1010 in binary. Other patterns represent different values.

questions.q: Which source would most likely produce data for a web analytics dashboard?
choices: A paper survey mailed once a decade
Handwritten receipts kept in a back room
Server and browser log files recording page visits
questions.explain: Web analytics relies on automatically generated server and browser logs, which record visits in near real time.

questions.q: Which stage of the data science process comes first?
choices: Defining the business question or problem
questions.explain: Data science projects start by defining the question, which determines what data is needed and how it will be analyzed.

questions.q: Why is data wrangling important?
choices: It replaces the need to collect data
Raw data is often messy and must be cleaned and transformed before analysis
It guarantees the model will be accurate
It is needed only after a model is deployed
questions.explain: Wrangling (cleaning, reshaping, and transforming) prepares raw data for analysis, and it usually takes a large share of project time.

questions.q: Which stage of the data science process involves communicating insights to stakeholders?
questions.explain: Communicating findings clearly is the final stage, where visualizations and summaries turn analysis into decisions.

questions.q: Which column in a CSV contains continuous numeric data?
questions.explain: Purchase totals can take any value in a range, so they are continuous. Cities and countries are categorical, and IDs are labels.

questions.q: A column records whether a customer subscribed, as yes or no. What type of data is this?
questions.explain: A yes/no flag has two categories and no numeric meaning, which makes it binary categorical data.

questions.q: What best describes data science?
choices: A branch of hardware engineering focused on storage chips
An interdisciplinary field that uses statistics, programming, and domain knowledge to extract insight from data
The study of probability theory alone
A method for manually recording paper surveys
questions.explain: Data science combines statistics, computing, and subject knowledge to turn data into insight and decisions.

questions.q: Which source is the best source of retail transaction data?
questions.explain: Point-of-sale systems record each sale as it happens, so their exports contain the transactions a retailer needs.

questions.q: Convert the binary number 1101 0110 to hexadecimal.
questions.explain: Group into nibbles: 1101 = D and 0110 = 6, giving D6. Reversing the nibbles gives 6D, a common mistake.

questions.q: What type of data is a series of temperatures recorded every hour?
questions.explain: Observations ordered over time at regular intervals form a time series, which needs time-aware analysis.

questions.q: Which of these is a common data quality dimension?
questions.explain: Completeness, accuracy, consistency, and timeliness are standard data quality dimensions.

questions.q: Which data format is most common for semi-structured data exchanged between web applications?
questions.explain: JSON stores key-value pairs in nested structures without a rigid table schema, which makes it semi-structured and widely used in web APIs.

questions.q: A dataset of 1,000 rows has 300 missing ages. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The dataset is unusable and must be discarded
The missing ages can safely be set to zero
The missingness rate is 30%, which should be investigated before choosing a handling method
Missing values only matter when computing the mean
questions.explain: A 30% missingness rate is large. Its cause determines whether imputation or other handling is valid, and zero-filling distorts results.

questions.q: Which step best describes data transformation?
choices: Storing data in a backup server
Converting values into a different form, such as scaling numbers or encoding categories
Publishing a report to a website
questions.explain: Transformation changes data representation for analysis, such as scaling numeric features or encoding categories as numbers.

questions.q: Which of these is inherently unstructured data?
choices: Video footage from a security camera
A list of employee IDs and salaries
questions.explain: Video has no predefined rows and columns. Inventory, salary, and address tables are structured.

vocab.def: The arithmetic average of a set of values, found by dividing their sum by the count of values.
The middle value of a sorted dataset, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even.
A measure of spread equal to the square root of the variance, in the same units as the data.
The average of the squared deviations from the mean, measuring how spread out the values are.
The probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes of a random variable.
A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution in which the mean, median, and mode are equal.
Two events where the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, so P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).
A measure of how two variables change together; positive values mean they tend to move in the same direction.
A variable that takes a countable set of separate values, such as whole-number counts.
A chart that groups a numeric variable into bins and shows how many observations fall in each bin.
vocab.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

vocab.def: A chart that displays the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and flags potential outliers.
vocab.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

vocab.def: A chart that plots pairs of numeric values as points, used to show the relationship between two variables.
vocab.sub: Data Analysis and Statistics for AI

vocab.def: Structured Query Language, the standard language for querying and managing data in relational databases.
A database that stores data in related tables linked by keys, queried with SQL.
A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row in a table and cannot be null.
A column in one table that references the primary key of another table to link related records.
A Python library that provides the DataFrame structure for loading, cleaning, and analyzing tabular data.
An open-source Python framework for building and training deep learning models.
The broad field of building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as reasoning, perception, and language.
AI models that create new content, such as text, images, audio, or code, based on patterns learned from training data.
A neural network trained on very large text datasets to predict and generate human language.
The AI subfield concerned with enabling computers to understand, analyze, and generate human language.
The AI subfield that enables computers to interpret and extract information from images and video.
AI designed to perform one specific task or a narrow set of tasks, in contrast to general AI.
The input text or instructions given to a generative AI model to guide the content it produces.
A branch of AI in which algorithms learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.
The portion of data used to fit a model's parameters during learning.
A held-out portion of data used to tune hyperparameters and compare models during development.
A held-out portion of data used once, at the end, to estimate how well a model performs on unseen data.
A learning approach that trains on labeled examples to predict known outcomes.
A learning approach that finds structure, such as clusters or patterns, in data without labels.
A learning approach in which an agent improves its actions by receiving rewards and penalties from its environment.
A subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn hierarchical representations.
A formal system that expresses statements about objects, their properties, and relations using quantifiers.
The logical symbol (for all) indicating that a statement holds for every element in a domain.
The logical symbol (there exists) indicating that a statement holds for at least one element in a domain.
A graphical model of random variables and their conditional dependencies, used to reason under uncertainty.
A graph whose edges have direction and contain no cycles; the structure underlying a Bayesian network.
The methods used to encode facts and relationships about the world so an AI system can reason over them.
Systematic and unfair outcomes produced by an algorithm, often reflecting bias in data or design.
Bias that already exists in the real-world data a model learns from, such as past discriminatory decisions.
A seemingly neutral feature that is correlated with a protected characteristic and can reproduce discrimination.
An AI output that is fluent and confident but factually unsupported or fabricated.
The practice of collecting and retaining only the personal data needed for a specific purpose.
An attribute, such as zip code or birth date, that does not identify someone alone but can identify them when combined with other data.
Data organized into a predefined schema of rows and columns with fixed fields, such as a relational table.
Data without a predefined schema, such as free text, images, audio, or video.
Data that has some organizational markers, such as tags or keys, without a rigid table schema, such as JSON.
A variable whose values are labels or groups rather than numeric quantities.
A variable whose values are numbers that support arithmetic, either continuous or discrete.
A base-2 number system using only the digits 0 and 1, which underlies how computers store data.
A base-16 number system using digits 0-9 and A-F, often used as a compact way to write binary values.
The process of cleaning, reshaping, and transforming raw data into a form suitable for analysis.
Observations recorded at successive points in time, analyzed with methods that account for ordering.
